concept: Service design, journey mapping and service blueprints

claims.text: Do not force substantially different observed journeys into one map. GOV.UK recommends a consolidated map when participants share stages and similar steps, and separate maps when groups have significantly different stages and steps. (low confidence)
Frog recommends testing a proposed service through prototypes before implementation so that risky assumptions encounter real users and real-world conditions. (low confidence)

A diagram should support investigation and change: blueprint dependencies can expose service weaknesses and redundant work. Nielsen Norman Group recommends prototyping future process changes before implementation and tracking changes against service goals. These are recommended uses, not proof that producing a diagram alone improves outcomes. (medium confidence)

Journey maps focus on customer actions, thoughts and feelings over time. Service blueprints connect customer actions to the organizational work that delivers the experience, rather than merely adding detail to the customer perspective. (medium confidence)

Keep hypothetical current-state maps, research-based current-state maps and proposed future-state maps distinct; research-based maps should describe what actually happens rather than what stakeholders want to happen. (low confidence)

Do not treat invented workshop personas as human evidence: a published workshop case explicitly invented an end-user, whereas government guidance requires research-based maps to reflect real users rather than stakeholder assumptions. (medium confidence)

Use blueprint dependencies and cross-team handoffs to locate candidate failure points; a diagram identifies where to investigate and improve service delivery rather than establishing an improvement outcome by itself. (medium confidence)

Mapping terminology varies: Smaply confines journey maps to the customer side of the line of visibility, while government practitioners allow journey-map layers for departments, teams and supporting back-end systems. Specify the layers and purpose rather than relying on the artifact name alone. (low confidence)

In blueprint terminology, evidence includes the props and places involved in service exchanges, such as physical stores, websites and emails; this layer can relate to both frontstage and backstage activity. This usage differs from research evidence used to substantiate a map. (medium confidence)

Scope a blueprint to a specific customer goal and scenario, align it with a business goal, and start with a focused problem. Smaply recommends expanding selected high-friction journey steps into operational layers instead of blueprinting every step by default. (medium confidence)

Ground current-experience maps in captured user experiences and research evidence instead of inventing customer actions or emotions. GOV.UK recommends event cards, relevant quotations, photos and research artefacts; Smaply likewise says maps and blueprints should be grounded in research rather than internal assumptions. (medium confidence)

Check the map against research and operational knowledge: review drafts with research observers and service-delivery teams, and involve knowledge holders from the blueprint phases and layers. For investigating failure points, Nielsen Norman Group recommends reviewing existing support tickets and other research, filling gaps, and combining attitudinal with behavioral evidence because reported behavior may differ from actual behavior. (medium confidence)
Service design organizes the people, resources and processes that deliver an experience; service blueprinting makes those delivery relationships visible for analysis and redesign. (medium confidence)

A blueprint links customer actions to frontstage actions visible to the customer, backstage actions performed out of view, and enabling support processes and systems. Frontstage interactions can involve staff or self-service technology. (medium confidence)

The line of interaction marks direct customer–organization interactions; the line of visibility separates visible frontstage activity from hidden backstage activity; the line of internal interaction separates contact work from deeper support functions. (medium confidence)

Blueprint evidence can mean physical or digital service cues such as signage, a website or an email inbox; this is distinct from the research observations, participant quotes and artefacts used to substantiate a map. (medium confidence)
Scope a blueprint to a specific journey, user goal and improvement objective; different scenarios within the same service may require separate blueprints. (low confidence)

Validate a draft map with research observers and teams who deliver the service, and involve frontline and support participants in examining blueprint steps for difficulties and problem areas. (medium confidence)

The digital-scribe case reports that blueprinting connected clinician actions and software processes for team communication, but its conclusions are exploratory and the project ended at conceptualization; it does not establish deployed service outcomes. (low confidence)

Nielsen Norman Group defines service design as organizing people, props and processes to improve employee experience and, indirectly, customer experience; it identifies blueprinting as a service-design mapping tool. (low confidence)

Nielsen Norman Group distinguishes current-state maps, which describe the existing experience, from future-state maps, which describe an ideal experience. It permits assumption-first hypothesis maps but warns that teams may stop before research validation and use hypotheses to make critical decisions; its hybrid approach follows the draft with user research and revision. (low confidence)

Treat journey maps and blueprints as maintained decision tools. Smaply warns that one-time deliverables go stale; GOV.UK recommends iteratively reviewing and revising draft maps until they accurately reflect user experience. (medium confidence)
